controls.note: Untrusted prose uses text nodes; JSON responses are serialized, headers use fixed categories. Trusted authored build HTML has a separate parser/CSP boundary. The Chessground 10.4.2 adaptation moves one fixed SVG style declaration into trusted CSS with exact-version/fragment build guards, preserving style-src-attr denial; no untrusted text is added.
Library sources accept HTTP(S) URLs without credentials; record IDs are encoded and chess links use checked positions. External navigation privacy is assessed separately.
API/library messages use JSON serialization rather than concatenating untrusted JavaScript. Imported data is not emitted as executable source.
Usage and library values use bound SQLite parameters. Fixed migration/schema SQL is application-owned; no client-selected SQL is accepted.
The runtime exposes no OS-command tool or client-controlled process invocation. Chess tools run fixed browser engine operations; operator build commands are trusted development actions.
No WYSIWYG or untrusted HTML rendering feature exists. PGN/model/library text is treated as text. parse5 parses trusted authored build input; it is not used as an untrusted HTML sanitizer.
No application path evaluates model, PGN or user text as JavaScript. Workers and WASM load trusted build/catalogue assets; tools use a fixed allowlist. This does not certify third-party internals.
No XML parser or user XML input exists. The shipped SVG icon is a trusted static asset.
The validation guide records expected structures, limits, browser/server responsibilities and references to authoritative source constants and tests.
Gateway roles/provider/consent/limits and server library IDs, revisions, PGN and source metadata are checked before security-relevant work.
The Node gateway enforces its own message/privacy/admission checks; library writes independently validate shared record rules and recompile PGN. Browser checks alone do not authorize writes.

Library mutations use current-owner revisions and transactions. Provider routing/consent is captured after body reads; stale browser work is rejected by session/position checks. No financial or account workflow exists.
Static/API responses have explicit types, nosniff and frame isolation. Public paths reject hidden/private data; API JSON is not served as HTML. SVG charset remains a separate open item.
Coach, imports and literal highlights use text nodes rather than HTML interpolation. Browser regressions exercise hostile markup and regex-like text.

Native TLS sends a __Host- session cookie with Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite=Strict/Path=/ and protected __Secure- collection locators at their canonical API paths, without Domain. Locators are adopted only with operator proof and do not authorize access. Migration preserves usage/library hashes, records, revisions and counters without rewriting their version-one schemas; the separate session registry is private. Explicit HTTP development remains a separate synthetic namespace outside final deployment. Backend termination is assessed separately; function permissions are assessed separately; endpoint trust/inventory and complete client cleanup retain their own gates.

Final native TLS uses the isolated kibitz.test authority (or an explicitly configured dedicated .test name) with exact DNS-SAN startup validation and operator loopback resolution. One-year HSTS is set before all application routes, including static/model/AI streams, HEAD and normal success/error responses. IP/localhost aliases expose only a static health manifest with no identity/HSTS; parser failures close without an outside-policy response. Forwarding headers cannot alter this policy; published ports retain full Origin checks. Native/custom-host/500/alias tests, built-browser tests, an independently trusted curl policy-cache/upgrade test and the actual default-command Linux image case pass at the reviewed source. Explicit HTTP development and original-origin TLS recovery are outside final deployment. No includeSubDomains/preload, automatic cross-host cookie transfer or operator browser trust/inventory claim is made.
The server does not emit Access-Control-Allow-Origin or reflect arbitrary origins. No wildcard-sensitive CORS response is enabled.
Sensitive writes require JSON and provider consent headers where applicable; library access additionally checks fetch metadata and full native Origin. Direct local non-browser clients remain trusted.

All AI write routes require JSON and a full Origin matching the native socket scheme/host. Wrong HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, blob and null Origins are rejected despite forwarding-header spoofing. Direct local clients without Origin remain trusted; preflight receives no CORS approval.

Provider work/configuration and library writes/erase require POST/DELETE as appropriate. GET status/read paths do not perform inference or mutate private records; minting a grouping cookie is not authentication.

JSON, NDJSON, HTML, JS, CSS, text and SVG responses declare UTF-8 with their corresponding media type. Actual CLI GET/HEAD and browser SVG document checks verify the former SVG gap; binary/unknown assets remain binary media types.
There is no WebSocket service/client. Coaching uses HTTP NDJSON, and in-page workers use local message channels.

There is no arbitrary file-upload endpoint. Pasted PGN/JSON is bounded separately. The operator model downloader enforces catalogue size, streaming byte limits and a total deadline before publication.

Model downloads use fixed GGUF catalogue names and verify exact length/hash before publication; cached files are scoped to the operator-controlled model directory. PGN content is parsed as chess data, not accepted by extension alone.

The static server reads descriptors as bytes and does not execute uploaded/generated data as Node code. Private library/usage files stay outside the static tree; catalogue model serving is narrowly scoped.

Static/model/private file boundaries reject traversal, hidden paths and symlink substitution; model filenames and fixture output names come from fixed allowlists. This is scoped to the implemented entry points.

The local operator sign-in policy documents a fixed ten-attempt per-process sixty-second window, foreign-origin rejection before counting, reset/restart behavior and no permanent account lockout state. A hostile process on the trusted local machine can still deny service; no adaptive service or hosted lockout policy is claimed. Operator secrets are generated 256-bit machine credentials, not human-chosen account passwords.

There are no user-set account passwords. Explicit offline setup generates a 256-bit installation key; its fixed base64url format is a machine-credential format, not a human password length policy. Hosted password authentication remains deferred.

There is no account password or browser password-change workflow. The local operator manages the private machine-key file; preserving its operator ID while replacing the secret and restarting invalidates the previous credential epoch. This scope does not claim a hosted password-change implementation.

No current/new account-password transaction exists. Administrative replacement of the private installation key is outside a browser password-change workflow; registry checks bind sessions to the configured operator and credential epoch.

No account registration/reset accepts human passwords. Explicit setup generates an unpredictable 256-bit machine key; a common-password denylist is not the policy for this key format. Do not replace it with a human-chosen password.

The application has no human account-password composition policy. The operator form accepts the exact fixed base64url machine-key format generated during explicit setup; this is not a user-password composition restriction.

No human/account password is collected. The installation-key form does conceal the high-entropy machine credential with a password-type input and clears it on submission/departure; this does not introduce a human password workflow.
No user-password enrolment/entry or password-manager contract exists. The local machine-key form permits paste; it does not register a hosted account password.
There is no received human account password to normalize. Machine keys are compared exactly in their documented fixed format; trimming or normalizing them would change the credential.

Native TLS, exact Host/Origin checks, bounded JSON proof and a fixed ten-attempt sixty-second sign-in window enforce the documented local machine-key policy. Tests reject bad proofs/foreign origins/oversized input, exercise 429, and advance the clock to confirm recovery without permanent operator disable. Private setup uses 256 random bits; hosted credential stuffing and adaptive risk services remain outside scope.

No factory/default operator account or key is supplied. Explicit private setup creates a new random operator ID and 256-bit secret; repeated initialization refuses overwrite. TLS API startup with absent/invalid operator configuration fails before database creation rather than opening anonymous access.

No temporary initial password or account activation code is issued. Explicit private setup generates a long-term 256-bit installation machine key, not a bootstrap password to be changed by a web account. Random session tokens are independently issued, replaced on reauthentication and expire at the backend.
No password hints or security-question authentication feature exists.

All supported HTTPS gateway/library functions resolve identity through the backend-issued token registry bound to the private local operator ID and credential epoch. Only a SHA-256 token verifier is stored; unknown, invented, duplicate, expired and different-operator tokens fail. Raw grouping locators never grant access; migration/recovery requires fresh operator proof and transactional ownership bindings. Native CLI/browser and actual default Linux image checks exercise this boundary. Explicit synthetic HTTP development and legacy-origin recovery remain outside final deployment; hosted accounts and authenticated client cleanup retain their own scope/TODOs. Explicit function authority is assessed separately under 8.2.1. Backend termination is assessed separately under 7.4.1.

Authentication issues a fresh random reference session token, separate from the installation key and collection locators. The key is used only for fresh operator proof; presenting it or a grouping value as a session cookie does not create a registered session.

Issued session tokens contain 32 CSPRNG bytes encoded as base64url. Registry lookup uses their SHA-256 verifier; token shape does not authorize access. Tests cover distinct issuance, strict cookie parsing, fabricated values, duplicate cookies and another operator. Usage/library locators are separate non-authorizing identifiers.

Successful authentication issues a fresh token. When reauthenticating with a previous session cookie, the registry removes that operator-owned previous token and inserts its replacement in the same transaction. It cannot remove a different operator’s token, and a failed issuance rolls back. Real TLS restart/recovery tests confirm the previous token returns 401 while the replacement retains the collection.

Native TLS logout deletes the presented operator/credential-bound backend session before acknowledgement, expires its host cookie and rejects copied-token replay across restart. Absolute persisted expiry is checked independently of browser cookies. Request guards recheck asynchronous work; short registry transactions serialize protected output/private mutation boundaries against revocation, without locks across awaited provider work. Active responses close on local termination, expiry or a bounded cross-process registry poll; uncancellable late provider output and paused private writes are denied. Actual CLI/second-process, browser and default Linux image tests verify these boundaries. Already emitted bytes, committed actions and provider-accepted work cannot be recalled; completed accepted usage can still be accounted for. Protected locators remain proof-authorized recovery inputs; complete authenticated client/offline cleanup remains TODO 11.4.2.11.

There is no hosted account registry or account disable/delete workflow. The private installation operator and credential epoch are verified at the backend; library erasure remains a separate data action. General backend logout/revocation is assessed under 7.4.1; this absence is specific to account disable/delete workflows.

Deployment/threat/permission documentation defines explicit function grants for the local operator, session-bound collection rules and read prerequisites for private mutation. Authentication, provider sharing consent and function/data authority remain separate. The private policy is bound to the operator ID, denies unknown functions and supports live revocation. Hosted accounts remain deferred; complete client lifecycle retains its own scope.

Every supported TLS gateway/library method and route requires an explicit grant from a private version-one policy bound to the authenticated local operator. Unmapped functions deny by default; library mutations also require read and retain current collection/scope/revision checks. Native startup validates policy before private storage/listening; bounded live policy reads at dispatch and protected output/mutation boundaries reject denied or unverifiable authorization before further use. Browser claims, sharing consent and raw grouping values cannot grant functions. Native CLI tests cover every empty/individual grant, unchanged denied data/usage, operator/collection boundaries and held-provider revocation; built English/German browser and default Linux image checks verify actual behavior. Provider consent/budgets and backend session lifecycle remain independent. Public/client-only resources and explicit synthetic HTTP development are outside final backend authorization; complete authenticated client/offline cleanup remains TODO 11.4.2.11.

TLS queries use the collection held in the verified operator session plus explicit read/mutation grants. Browser scope/record IDs or raw grouping locators cannot switch those claims; transactional collection bindings reject a different operator. Actual CLI tests preserve existing private records, reject cross-collection scope writes and reject other-operator session/adoption even with full grants. Explicit synthetic HTTP development remains outside final deployment.

Node checks backend-issued identity, explicit current operator function grants and collection/scope/revision/write rules at the trusted service layer. Browser grants/controls and sharing attestations cannot authorize functions. Direct TLS handlers without a trusted session permission guard fail closed; live denial or unverifiable policy blocks further protected output/mutation. Hosted authorization and complete authenticated client cleanup remain separate scope.
No self-contained authorization token is accepted. Grouping cookies are opaque references, not JWT claims.
No self-contained token creation/verification or client-selected token algorithm exists.
No JWT issuer, token-key URL or self-contained-token key resolution is implemented.
No self-contained token claims or nbf/exp fields are parsed; grouping-cookie lifecycle deviations are tracked separately.
Kibitz is not an OAuth/OIDC authorization server and has no authorization redirect endpoint.
There is no OAuth authorization-code issue/redemption operation.
No OAuth authorization codes are generated or accepted.
No OAuth grants are configured or processed. Server provider API authentication is not an application OAuth authorization server.
No OAuth refresh tokens, refresh endpoint or authorization grant state exists.
The application does not implement bulk/asymmetric encryption or select padding modes. Node/browser transport TLS is assessed separately; persisted local data is not encrypted by the app.
There is no application-managed encryption cipher suite to approve. This is not a claim about provider infrastructure or a guarantee of encryption at rest.
Reviewed application integrity/scope digests use SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-256; token entropy uses Node CSPRNG. Non-security retrieval signatures are not represented as cryptographic integrity.

Legacy attempts were refused by the local client, not established as peer refusal. The current source now enforces 1.2–1.3 listener/health settings and reviewed outbound runtime defaults, with verified local SDK TLS 1.3 fixtures and source-pinned image tests. Actual operator/browser/provider/CDN endpoint negotiations and complete downgrade-refusal evidence remain unverified; no release deployment was inspected. Provider/coaching/connection-test/embedding/Ollama inspection destinations require HTTPS and reviewed runtime TLS defaults, and all provider redirects are refused before forwarding keys or context. Only explicit development permits exact loopback HTTP. Browser weight URLs are app-relative; model provisioning validates its initial HTTPS source before filesystem creation and every bounded HTTPS redirect before its socket, retaining pinned publication checks. Health peer verification cannot inherit an ambient TLS-disable flag. Actual local SDK TLS fixtures, the pre-enforcement CLI regression, 17 affected browser cases and the strengthened source-pinned actual Linux image case verify these boundaries.
